title: A data year has two clocks
subtitle: Calendar age and lag from an indicator's production frontier send different cells to review.
finding: At a three-year rule, 138 of 709 observed cells (19.5%) change review status when calendar age is replaced by lag from the indicator's own global production frontier—all of them calendar-only flags.
finding_short: 19.5% of observed cells change review status when the second clock is used.
limits: Does not rate economies, statistical offices, data quality, or formal release standards.
Threshold-dependent: disagreement is 52.6% at two effective years and 0.7% at five.
Removing environment and climate drops disagreement to 9.2%, below the 10% gate—so the claim stays domain-concentrated.
key_messages: A latest-year label mixes shared production age with economy-specific lag.
All 138 disagreements are calendar-only; none are relative-only at the baseline rule.
Environment, health, and education account for nearly all disagreement; the cross-domain claim does not hold.

sections.title: The problem with a single age label
sections.body: A development dashboard often paints a cell by its latest reference year. That single label answers how old the phenomenon is, but not whether the economy trails what the indicator currently makes possible.

sections.title: What the panel shows
sections.body: In a prospectively frozen panel of 42 ADB developing member economies and 18 World Development Indicators, 138 of 709 observed cells (19.5%) change three-year review status when calendar age is replaced by lag from the indicator's own global production frontier. All 138 are calendar-only flags.

sections.title: Why the claim narrows
sections.body: Environment and climate contributes 80 of the 138 disagreements; health 40; education 11. Removing environment drops disagreement to 9.2%, below the 10% decision gate. The supported conclusion is domain-aware.

sections.title: How the clocks are defined
sections.body: Calendar age equals indicator-wide production age plus economy-specific relative lag. The absolute rule flags cells with calendar age at least three years; the relative rule flags cells three or more years behind the indicator's global frontier.

sections.title: What survives and what does not
sections.body: Disagreement stays above 10% in frozen 9-, 18-, and 27-indicator sets. Magnitude is highly threshold-dependent. Domain deletion reshapes interpretation, not the construct distinction.

workbench_rows.label: Environment and climate
workbench_rows.note: All observed cells are calendar-old; none trail the frontier by three years.

workbench_rows.label: Health
workbench_rows.note: Half of observed cells are calendar-old and source-current at the rule.

workbench_rows.label: Education
workbench_rows.note: Both clocks flag some cells; 11 disagreements remain production-cycle only.

workbench_rows.label: Poverty and inequality
workbench_rows.note: Oldest median calendar age (5 years); most old cells also trail the frontier.

workbench_rows.label: Labor and social conditions
workbench_rows.note: Highest missing share (16.7%); missing is not old.

workbench_rows.label: Infrastructure and digital access
workbench_rows.note: Both clocks agree on the review set.

workbench_rows.label: Economy and structure
workbench_rows.note: Almost no review pressure at three years.

workbench_rows.label: Demography
workbench_rows.note: No three-year review flags on either clock.

non_claim: This is an economy-by-indicator measurement and coverage diagnostic. It is not a rating of an economy, statistical office, data quality, or formal dissemination timeliness.
